stimuli.text: Researchers grew a population of duckweed plants in a container with a fixed supply of resources and counted the population every two days.
Students placed potato cores of equal mass in sucrose solutions of different concentrations at 22 °C. After 24 hours, they measured each core's percent change in mass.

In liver cells, the hormone epinephrine binds a G protein-coupled receptor. The activated G protein activates adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to cyclic AMP (cAMP). cAMP activates protein kinase A, which starts a phosphorylation cascade that leads to the breakdown of glycogen into glucose. An enzyme in the cell breaks down cAMP.

In a population of 500 beetles, long wings (allele B) is dominant to short wings (allele b). Researchers count 125 beetles with short wings. Assume the population is in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1).
Two pea plants heterozygous for height (T, tall, dominant) and flower color (P, purple, dominant) were crossed, producing 160 offspring.

questions.stem: A diploid cell has 14 chromosomes (2n = 14). How many chromatids are present in the cell during G2?

options.why: Mitosis does not halve the chromosome number.
Check whether DNA has been replicated at this point.
Correct. After S phase each chromosome has two sister chromatids.
Replication doubles the chromatids only once.

questions.explanation: 14 chromosomes; chromatid count is 28 in G2.

questions.stem: An inhibitor reduces an enzyme's rate, but adding a large amount of substrate restores the maximum rate. What kind of inhibitor is it?

options.why: Cofactors help enzymes work.
Denaturation is not reversed by substrate.
Correct. Excess substrate outcompetes an inhibitor for the active site.
Extra substrate cannot overcome allosteric inhibition.

questions.explanation: Excess substrate outcompetes an inhibitor for the active site.

questions.stem: Which molecule can diffuse directly across a phospholipid bilayer most easily?

options.why: Correct. Small nonpolar molecules pass through the hydrophobic core.
Ions are repelled by the hydrophobic core.
Proteins are too large.
Glucose is large and polar.

questions.explanation: Small nonpolar molecules pass through the hydrophobic core.

questions.stem: Which observation best supports the RNA world hypothesis?

options.text: DNA is more stable than RNA
options.why: That explains why DNA took over later.

options.text: Proteins are made of amino acids
options.why: That does not support the hypothesis.
That is not specific to RNA.

options.text: Some RNA molecules can catalyze reactions as well as store information
options.why: Correct. RNA can serve both roles.

questions.explanation: RNA can serve both roles.

questions.stem: A small group of birds colonizes an island, and an allele rare on the mainland becomes common there. What explains this?

options.why: Allele frequencies changed.
This is chance, not selection.
Correct. A few founders carried, by chance, a different set of alleles.
Gene flow would make populations more similar.

questions.explanation: A few founders carried, by chance, a different set of alleles.

questions.stem: What is the average rate of product formation between 0 and 6 minutes?

options.why: Correct. Rate is the change in product divided by the change in time.
Recheck the time interval.
Divide by the time elapsed.
Rate is Δproduct ÷ Δtime, not the inverse.

questions.stem: A plant cell has a water potential of -0.97 MPa. It is placed in a solution with a water potential of -1.1 MPa. Which describes the net movement of water?

options.text: Out of the cell, because water moves toward higher water potential
options.why: Water moves toward lower water potential.

options.text: Into the cell, because the cell has the higher water potential
options.why: Water moves from higher to lower water potential.

options.text: No net movement, because water potential does not affect osmosis
options.why: Differences in water potential drive osmosis.

options.text: Out of the cell, because water moves toward the lower (more negative) water potential
options.why: Correct. Water moves from -0.97 MPa to -1.1 MPa.

questions.explanation: Water flows from higher to lower water potential: from the cell into the solution.

questions.stem: A steroid hormone affects target cells but not other cells. Which best explains this?

options.why: Steroids cross membranes.

options.text: Only target cells contain the specific intracellular receptor
options.why: Correct. Responses require the right receptor.

options.text: Other cells destroy the hormone immediately
options.why: Specificity comes from receptors.

options.text: Only target cells have a plasma membrane
options.why: All cells do.

questions.explanation: Responses require the right receptor.

questions.stem: The producers in an ecosystem store 50,000 kcal of energy. Assuming about 10% transfer between trophic levels, about how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?

options.why: Count the number of transfers from producers.
About 10% is passed on; about 90% is lost.
Count the number of transfers from producers.
Correct. 2 transfers of 10% each.

questions.explanation: Each level keeps about 10%: 50,000 × 0.1^2 = 500 kcal.

questions.stem: Bacteria release a signaling molecule and begin forming a biofilm only when the population is dense. What is this called?

options.why: Correct. Signals accumulate to a threshold at high density.
That is programmed cell death.
That is cell division.
That uses hormones in animals.

questions.explanation: Signals accumulate to a threshold at high density.

questions.stem: Two cube-shaped cells have side lengths of 3 µm and 10 µm. Which statement correctly compares their surface area-to-volume ratios?

options.text: The 10 µm cell has the greater ratio, 60, so it exchanges materials more efficiently
options.why: SA:V decreases as size increases.

options.text: The 3 µm cell has a ratio of 2, which is greater than the 10 µm cell's 0.6, so it exchanges materials more efficiently
options.why: Correct. For a cube, SA:V = 6s²/s³ = 6/s.

options.text: Both cells have the same ratio, 6, because both are cubes
options.why: The ratio depends on side length.

options.text: The 3 µm cell has a ratio of 2, which is greater, so it exchanges materials less efficiently
options.why: A greater ratio means more surface per unit volume: more efficient exchange.

questions.explanation: SA:V = 6/s: 2 for 3 µm and 0.6 for 10 µm. Smaller cells have more surface area per unit volume.

questions.stem: On a phylogenetic tree, what does a node represent?

options.why: Tips represent living species.

options.text: The most recent common ancestor of the lineages that branch from it
options.why: Correct. Nodes are branch points.

options.text: An extinct species with no descendants
options.why: Nodes have descendants.

options.text: The time of a mass extinction
options.why: Nodes mark divergence.

questions.explanation: Nodes are branch points.

questions.stem: Blood glucose rises after a meal, insulin is released and glucose falls. What does this illustrate?

options.why: That is bacterial communication.
Correct. The response reverses the change.
Positive feedback amplifies a change.
This is a feedback loop.

questions.explanation: The response reverses the change.

questions.stem: Which feature allows carbon to form the backbone of diverse biological molecules?

options.why: Carbon readily bonds with oxygen.

options.text: It can form four covalent bonds, building chains, branches and rings
options.why: Correct. Carbon's bonding versatility allows many structures.

options.text: It forms ionic bonds with hydrogen
options.why: Carbon–hydrogen bonds are covalent.

options.text: It is the most abundant element in water
options.why: Water contains no carbon.

questions.explanation: Carbon's bonding versatility allows many structures.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 21% cytosine. What percentage of the bases are adenine?

options.why: 21% is the amount of guanine, which pairs with cytosine.
Correct. guanine also makes up 21%; the remaining 58% is split equally between the other two bases.
That is the total for both remaining bases together.
Both members of each base pair must be accounted for.

questions.explanation: By base pairing, cytosine = guanine = 21%. The other two bases share 58%, so each is 29%.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 29% cytosine. What percentage of the bases are thymine?

options.why: Correct. guanine also makes up 29%; the remaining 42% is split equally between the other two bases.
29% is the amount of guanine, which pairs with cytosine.
That is the total for both remaining bases together.
Both members of each base pair must be accounted for.

questions.stem: What is the average rate of product formation between 0 and 6 minutes?

options.why: Correct. Rate is the change in product divided by the change in time.

Rate is Δproduct ÷ Δtime, not the inverse.

questions.stem: An organism has a diploid number of 6. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can it produce by independent assortment?

options.why: Combinations multiply: each pair has 2 orientations.
Correct. With 3 homologous pairs, there are 2^3 combinations.
The count is 2 raised to the number of pairs.
The number of pairs is 3, not 6.

questions.explanation: n = 3 pairs, each with two orientations at metaphase I: 2^3 = 8.

questions.stem: A diploid cell has 14 chromosomes (2n = 14). How many chromatids are present in the cell during G1?

options.why: Mitosis does not halve the chromosome number.
Correct. Before S phase (and after division) each chromosome is a single chromatid.
Check whether DNA has been replicated at this point.
Replication doubles the chromatids only once.

questions.explanation: 14 chromosomes; chromatid count is 14 in G1.

questions.stem: One strand of DNA reads 5′-GGCCCATT-3′. What is the sequence of the complementary strand, written 5′ to 3′?

options.why: Each base must be paired, not just reversed.
DNA contains T, not U.
The complementary strand is antiparallel; written 5′ to 3′ it is reversed.
Correct. Pair each base and reverse the direction, because strands are antiparallel.

questions.explanation: The complement of 5′-GGCCCATT-3′ is 3′-CCGGGTAA-5′, written 5′-AATGGGCC-3′.

questions.stem: The rate of glucose uptake into a cell increases with glucose concentration but levels off at high concentrations, and no ATP is used. What explains this?

options.text: Facilitated diffusion through a limited number of carrier proteins
options.why: Correct. Carriers become saturated.
No ATP is used.
That releases materials.

questions.explanation: Carriers become saturated.

questions.stem: Pill bugs move faster and turn less in dry areas and slow down in moist areas, ending up mostly in moist areas. This behavior is:

options.why: That is plant growth toward light.
Taxis is directed movement.
That is long-distance seasonal movement.
Correct. A change in speed of random movement.

questions.explanation: A change in speed of random movement.

questions.stem: How does an enzyme speed up a reaction?

options.text: It raises the temperature of the cell
options.why: Enzymes do not heat the cell.

options.text: It increases the energy released by the reaction
options.why: ΔG is unchanged.
Correct. Enzymes lower the energy barrier without changing ΔG.

options.text: It is used up as a reactant
options.why: Enzymes are not consumed.

questions.explanation: Enzymes lower the energy barrier without changing ΔG.

questions.stem: Based on the data, which two species most likely share the most recent common ancestor among species W, X, Y, Z?

options.why: They differ by 18, more than X and Z.
They differ by 7, more than X and Z.
Correct. They have the fewest differences (6).
They differ by 20, more than X and Z.

questions.explanation: Fewer sequence differences indicate more recent divergence: X and Z differ by only 6.

questions.stem: The producers in an ecosystem store 150,000 kcal of energy. Assuming about 10% transfer between trophic levels, about how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?

options.why: Correct. 2 transfers of 10% each.

Count the number of transfers from producers.

questions.explanation: Each level keeps about 10%: 150,000 × 0.1^2 = 1,500 kcal.

questions.stem: A plant cell has a water potential of -0.93 MPa. It is placed in a solution with a water potential of -0.2 MPa. Which describes the net movement of water?

options.text: No net movement, because water potential does not affect osmosis
options.why: Differences in water potential drive osmosis.

options.text: Out of the cell, because the cell has the lower water potential

options.text: Into the cell, because water moves toward higher water potential
options.why: Water moves toward lower water potential.

options.text: Into the cell, because water moves toward the lower (more negative) water potential

questions.explanation: Water flows from higher to lower water potential: from the solution into the cell.

questions.stem: 297 glucose molecules are joined into one linear polysaccharide by dehydration synthesis. How many water molecules are released?

options.why: Correct. A chain of 297 monomers has 296 bonds, and each bond involves one water molecule.
There is one fewer bond than monomers in a linear chain.
There is one fewer bond than monomers.
Each bond involves one water molecule, not two.

questions.explanation: Linking 297 monomers forms 296 bonds; each releases one water molecule.

questions.stem: A PCR reaction starts with 1 copy of a target DNA sequence. Assuming each cycle doubles the DNA, how many copies are present after 23 cycles?

options.why: There are 23 doublings.
Growth is exponential with base 2.
Correct. Each cycle doubles the number of copies.
Copies double each cycle; they do not increase by 2.

questions.explanation: After 23 doublings: 1 × 2^23 copies.

questions.stem: One strand of DNA reads 5′-ATCGAAAG-3′. What is the sequence of the complementary strand, written 5′ to 3′?

DNA contains T, not U.

questions.stem: The producers in an ecosystem store 100,000 kcal of energy. Assuming about 10% transfer between trophic levels, about how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?

Count the number of transfers from producers.

questions.explanation: Each level keeps about 10%: 100,000 × 0.1^2 = 1,000 kcal.

questions.stem: The producers in an ecosystem store 80,000 kcal of energy. Assuming about 10% transfer between trophic levels, about how much energy is available to the secondary consumers?

options.why: Count the number of transfers from producers.

questions.stem: A researcher supplies cells with radioactive nitrogen. Which molecules will become labeled?

options.why: These contain only C, H and O.
Correct. Nitrogen is in amino groups and nitrogenous bases.
Water contains no nitrogen.
Phospholipids contain phosphorus, but proteins and nucleic acids hold most nitrogen.

questions.explanation: Nitrogen is in amino groups and nitrogenous bases.

questions.stem: An antibiotic is used to treat an infection, and resistant bacteria become common. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Each bacterium learned to resist the drug
options.why: Individuals do not adapt this way.

options.text: Resistant bacteria were present before treatment and survived to reproduce
options.why: Correct. The antibiotic selected existing variants.

options.text: The antibiotic caused the mutations for resistance
options.why: Mutations arise randomly.

options.text: Resistance spreads only through the patient's immune system
options.why: Resistance spreads through bacterial reproduction and gene transfer.

questions.explanation: The antibiotic selected existing variants.

questions.stem: Which condition would cause allele frequencies to change, violating Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?

options.why: Random mating is a condition for equilibrium.

options.text: Individuals with one allele produce more offspring than others
options.why: Correct. That is natural selection.
No migration is a condition for equilibrium.
Large size is a condition for equilibrium.

questions.explanation: That is natural selection.

questions.stem: Cyanide blocks the final protein of the electron transport chain in mitochondria. Which is the most immediate effect?

options.text: The proton gradient is no longer maintained, so ATP synthase makes much less ATP
options.why: Correct. Electrons cannot pass to oxygen, so pumping stops.
ATP production falls.
Glycolysis can continue briefly.
Oxygen is no longer reduced.

questions.explanation: Electrons cannot pass to oxygen, so pumping stops.

questions.stem: The forelimbs of humans, bats and whales have the same bone pattern but different functions. These are:

options.text: Analogous structures, evidence of convergent evolution
options.why: Analogous structures have different origins.
They support evolution.
They are functional.

options.text: Homologous structures, evidence of common ancestry
options.why: Correct. Shared structure from a common ancestor.

questions.explanation: Shared structure from a common ancestor.

questions.stem: In a population, individuals of intermediate size have the highest survival, and the range of sizes narrows over generations. What type of selection is this?

options.why: Correct. The intermediate phenotype is favored.
That favors both extremes.
That favors one extreme.
Drift is random, not based on traits.

questions.explanation: The intermediate phenotype is favored.

questions.stem: Why is the lagging strand synthesized as Okazaki fragments?

options.text: Helicase works only on one strand
options.why: Helicase unwinds both.

options.text: Ligase cuts the strand into fragments
options.why: Ligase joins fragments.

options.text: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to the 3′ end, and the strands are antiparallel
options.why: Correct. The lagging strand must be built away from the fork.

options.text: The lagging strand is made of RNA
options.why: It is DNA, built after RNA primers.

questions.explanation: The lagging strand must be built away from the fork.

questions.stem: A diploid cell has 20 chromosomes (2n = 20). How many chromatids are present in the cell during G2?

options.why: Mitosis does not halve the chromosome number.

Correct. After S phase each chromosome has two sister chromatids.

questions.stem: In the lac operon, what happens when lactose is present and glucose is absent?

options.text: The repressor binds the operator more tightly
options.why: Lactose inactivates the repressor.
Expression increases.
Regulation does not delete genes.

options.text: Lactose binds the repressor, which releases the operator, and the genes are transcribed

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 37% guanine. What percentage of the bases are thymine?

options.why: Correct. cytosine also makes up 37%; the remaining 26% is split equally between the other two bases.
That is the total for both remaining bases together.
37% is the amount of cytosine, which pairs with guanine.

questions.stem: A circular plasmid of 5000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1700 and 3400. The fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis. Which bands appear, and which travels farthest?

options.text: 1700 bp and 3300 bp; the 1700 bp band travels farthest
options.why: Correct. Two cuts in a circle give two pieces; smaller fragments move farther.

options.text: 1700 bp, 1700 bp and 1600 bp; the 1600 bp band travels farthest
options.why: A circular plasmid cut twice gives two fragments, not three.
The plasmid is cut into pieces.

options.text: 1700 bp and 3300 bp; the 3300 bp band travels farthest
options.why: Smaller fragments move through the gel more easily.

questions.explanation: The fragments are 3400 − 1700 = 1700 bp and 5000 − 1700 = 3300 bp.

questions.stem: What is the average rate of product formation between 2 and 6 minutes?

questions.stem: Why can yeast continue to make some ATP without oxygen?

options.text: Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue
options.why: Correct. Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ to keep running.

options.text: The Krebs cycle runs without oxygen
options.why: It depends on NAD⁺ from the electron transport chain.

options.text: Fermentation produces more ATP than respiration
options.why: It produces far less.
Yeast is not photosynthetic.

questions.explanation: Glycolysis needs NAD⁺ to keep running.

questions.stem: How does a phosphorylation cascade amplify a signal?

options.why: It produces a response, not ligand.
One ligand binds one receptor.

options.text: Each activated kinase activates many molecules at the next step
options.why: Correct. Each step multiplies the number of active molecules.
Phosphatases remove them.

questions.explanation: Each step multiplies the number of active molecules.

questions.stem: A dihybrid test cross produces 45% AB, 45% ab, 5% Ab and 5% aB offspring. What do these results suggest?

options.text: The genes are on different chromosomes
options.why: That gives a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.
Recombinants did appear.
That would give about 25% each.

options.text: The genes are linked, about 10 map units apart
options.why: Correct. Recombinants are 10% of offspring.

questions.explanation: Recombinants are 10% of offspring.

questions.stem: Using Simpson's diversity index, SDI = 1 − Σ(n/N)², what is the diversity of this sample?

options.why: Subtract the sum from 1.

The species are not equally abundant; use each species' own proportion.

questions.stem: Which best explains the change in rate between 45 °C and 65 °C?

options.text: High temperature disrupted the enzyme's shape, so fewer active sites could bind substrate
options.why: Correct. Above the optimum, the enzyme denatures.

options.text: The enzyme's activation energy increased because more substrate was added
options.why: Activation energy is not changed by adding substrate.

options.text: Molecules moved more slowly, so there were fewer collisions
options.why: Molecules move faster at higher temperatures.

options.text: The substrate was used up at high temperatures
options.why: The drop reflects the enzyme, not the supply of substrate.

questions.explanation: The rate peaks at 45 °C and falls sharply above it, consistent with denaturation of the enzyme.

questions.stem: Assuming independent assortment, what is the probability that a cross of AaBbCc × AaBbCc produces an offspring with the genotype or phenotype aabbcc?

options.why: Multiply the separate probabilities for each gene.
Multiply the separate probabilities for each gene.
Multiply the separate probabilities for each gene.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 49% of individuals show a recessive phenotype. What is the proportion of individuals heterozygous?

options.why: Use p² + 2pq + q² = 1 with q from the square root.

Take the square root of q² first.

options.why: Recheck the ionization constant.

Solute potential is negative: adding solute lowers water potential.

questions.stem: A recessive trait is X-linked. A carrier woman and an unaffected man have a daughter. What is the probability that the daughter is affected?

options.why: Track which X each parent can pass on.
Track which X each parent can pass on.
Track which X each parent can pass on.
Correct. Daughters need a recessive X from each parent.

questions.explanation: A daughter gets the father's only X (dominant) and one of the mother's: probability 0.

questions.stem: A point mutation changes the mRNA codon GGC to GGU. Which type of mutation is this?

options.text: Silent: the amino acid is unchanged
options.why: Correct. GGC codes for Gly and GGU for Gly.

options.text: Nonsense: an early stop codon shortens the protein
options.why: GGU is not a stop codon.

options.text: Missense: one amino acid is replaced
options.why: Both codons code for the same amino acid.

options.text: Frameshift: the reading frame is shifted
options.why: A substitution does not shift the reading frame.

questions.explanation: GGC (Gly) → GGU (Gly): a silent mutation.

Include the (K − N)/K factor for logistic growth.
Use the current size N.

options.why: Multiply the separate probabilities for each gene.

questions.stem: The template strand of a DNA segment reads 3′-TACCTCCGGACCATC-5′. Using the codon table, what polypeptide does it encode?

A stop codon does not add an amino acid.

questions.stem: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 9% of individuals show a recessive phenotype. What is the frequency of the dominant allele?

options.why: That is the recessive frequency itself.
Heterozygotes are 2pq.
Correct. q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7.

questions.stem: A cross is expected to produce offspring in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio. The observed counts are 117, 31, 39, 13 (total 200). Using a chi-square test at p = 0.05 (critical values: 3.84 for 1 df, 5.99 for 2 df, 7.81 for 3 df), which conclusion is correct?

options.text: χ² ≈ 1.39; the data prove the hypothesis is true
options.why: A chi-square test cannot prove a hypothesis.
Compare χ² with the critical value 7.81.

options.text: χ² ≈ 1.39; fail to reject the null hypothesis
options.why: Correct. With 3 df the critical value is 7.81; χ² is less, so the deviation can be explained by chance.

options.text: χ² ≈ 1.62; fail to reject the null hypothesis
options.why: Divide by the expected count, not the observed count.

questions.explanation: Expected counts: 112.5, 37.5, 37.5, 12.5. χ² = Σ(o − e)²/e ≈ 1.39 with 3 df, compared with 7.81.

parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the experiment, and identify one variable that should be held constant.

rubric.criterion: Independent variable: pH.
rubric.example: The pH of the buffer.

rubric.criterion: Dependent variable: initial reaction rate.
rubric.example: Rate of glucose production.

rubric.criterion: A valid controlled variable.
rubric.example: Temperature, enzyme concentration, substrate concentration or volume.

parts.prompt: Calculate the percent change in reaction rate when the pH changes from 8 to 6.

rubric.criterion: Correct calculation.

parts.prompt: Explain why the reaction rate is low at pH 4 and pH 12.

rubric.criterion: Extreme pH changes the charges on amino acid R groups.
rubric.example: H⁺ concentration alters ionic and hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape.

rubric.criterion: The active site's shape changes (denaturation), so substrate binds poorly.
rubric.example: Fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form, lowering the rate.

parts.prompt: The student repeats the experiment at pH 8 with twice as much enzyme and the same amount of substrate. Predict the effect on the initial rate, and justify your prediction.

rubric.criterion: Predicts the initial rate increases.
rubric.example: Higher than 50 µmol/min, up to about double.

rubric.criterion: Justifies with more active sites available when substrate is plentiful.
rubric.example: More enzyme molecules can bind substrate at the same time.

parts.prompt: A competitive inhibitor is added to the reaction at the optimal pH. Describe how increasing the substrate concentration would affect the inhibition, and explain why.

rubric.criterion: Inhibition decreases at high substrate concentration.
rubric.example: The rate approaches the uninhibited maximum.

rubric.criterion: Explains competition for the active site.
rubric.example: Substrate molecules outcompete the inhibitor for the active site.

parts.prompt: Describe how you would construct an appropriate graph of the data: the type of graph, the axes and their labels, and the scale.

rubric.criterion: Line or scatter graph with time on the x-axis.
rubric.example: Day on the x-axis, population size on the y-axis.

rubric.criterion: Axes labeled with units and linear scales; points plotted accurately and connected.
rubric.example: y-axis from 0 to at least 496.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of population growth between day 4 and day 8.

rubric.criterion: Correct calculation with units.
rubric.example: (395 − 127) ÷ 4 = 67 individuals per day

parts.prompt: Identify the type of population growth shown and estimate the carrying capacity.

rubric.criterion: Logistic growth.
rubric.example: An S-shaped curve that levels off.

rubric.criterion: Carrying capacity estimate consistent with the data.
rubric.example: About 500.

parts.prompt: Explain why the growth rate decreases as the population approaches the carrying capacity.

rubric.criterion: Identifies a density-dependent factor.
rubric.example: Competition for limited food and space, or buildup of wastes.

rubric.criterion: Links it to lower birth rates or higher death rates.
rubric.example: As density rises, fewer resources per individual reduce reproduction and survival.

parts.prompt: The researchers repeat the experiment with double the food supply. Predict the effect on the carrying capacity and justify your prediction.

rubric.criterion: Predicts a higher carrying capacity.
rubric.example: Greater than about 500.

rubric.criterion: Justifies: food was a limiting resource.
rubric.example: More resources allow the environment to support more individuals.

parts.prompt: Identify an appropriate control for the experiment, and explain why the students measured percent change rather than change in mass.

rubric.criterion: The 0 M (distilled water) treatment, or cores with no solution change.
rubric.example: Distilled water.

rubric.criterion: Percent change allows comparison of cores with slightly different starting masses.
rubric.example: It standardizes for initial mass.

parts.prompt: Estimate the sucrose concentration that is isotonic to the potato cells, and calculate the solute potential of that solution (Ψs = −iCRT, R = 0.0831, T in kelvins).

rubric.criterion: Isotonic concentration where the change in mass is zero.
rubric.example: About 0.24 M, interpolating between 0.2 and 0.4 M.

rubric.criterion: Solute potential calculated correctly from the estimate.

parts.prompt: Explain the change in mass of the cores in the 0.8 M solution.

rubric.criterion: Water moved out of the cells by osmosis toward the lower water potential of the solution.
rubric.example: The solution is hypertonic, so the cells lost water and mass.

parts.prompt: Describe the role of cAMP in this pathway.

rubric.criterion: cAMP is a second messenger that relays and amplifies the signal inside the cell.
rubric.example: It activates protein kinase A.

parts.prompt: Explain how a single epinephrine molecule can cause the release of a large number of glucose molecules.

rubric.criterion: Amplification: each activated enzyme activates many molecules at the next step.
rubric.example: One adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP; each kinase phosphorylates many targets.

parts.prompt: A mutation alters adenylyl cyclase, so that it cannot make cAMP. Predict the effect on glycogen breakdown, and justify your prediction.

rubric.criterion: Correct prediction.
rubric.example: Glycogen is not broken down in response to epinephrine.

rubric.criterion: Justification using the pathway.
rubric.example: Without the second messenger, protein kinase A is not activated.

parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency of the b allele and the expected number of heterozygous beetles.

rubric.criterion: q from the recessive phenotype frequency.
Expected heterozygotes.

parts.prompt: Identify two conditions that must be met for the population to remain in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

rubric.criterion: Two correct conditions.
rubric.example: A large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, no natural selection.

parts.prompt: Birds that prey on the beetles find beetles with long wings more easily on the new background. Predict how the frequency of the b allele will change over several generations, and justify your prediction.

rubric.criterion: Predicts q increases.
rubric.example: Beetles with short wings (bb) survive and reproduce more.

rubric.criterion: Justifies with differential survival and reproduction.
rubric.example: Selection removes B alleles faster, because both BB and Bb beetles are eaten more.

parts.prompt: State the null hypothesis, and calculate the expected number of offspring in each category.

rubric.criterion: Null hypothesis: the genes assort independently, giving a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
rubric.example: Any differences are due to chance.

rubric.criterion: Expected counts.

parts.prompt: Calculate the chi-square value and determine whether to reject the null hypothesis at p = 0.05 (critical value 7.81 for 3 degrees of freedom).

rubric.criterion: Correct chi-square value.
Correct conclusion with comparison to the critical value.
rubric.example: 2.53 is less than 7.81, so fail to reject the null hypothesis.

parts.prompt: Propose an explanation for the results.

rubric.criterion: Explanation consistent with the conclusion.
rubric.example: The genes assort independently; deviations are due to chance.
